notes.definition: A way of building programs that learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules.
notes.example: **Machine learning** lets your phone recognize faces without anyone writing a rule for every face.

notes.definition: The field of making computers do tasks that normally require human intelligence.
notes.example: **AI** is already part of everyday tools like maps and translators.
notes.note: AI читается /ˌeɪ ˈaɪ/. Без артикля: «AI is…», не «the AI is…» (если речь о сфере в целом).

notes.definition: A collection of examples used to train or test a model.
notes.example: We collected a **dataset** of 10,000 labeled photos.
notes.note: data в ML часто неисчисляемое: the data is… (в научных текстах встречается и the data are…).

notes.definition: One single example in a dataset.
notes.example: Each **data point** represents one customer.

notes.definition: A measurable property of the input that a model uses to make predictions.
notes.example: Age and income turned out to be the most important **features**.

notes.definition: The correct answer attached to a training example.
notes.example: Every email in the training set has a **label**: spam or not spam.

notes.definition: The real, verified answers that a model's predictions are compared with.
notes.example: We compared the predictions with the **ground truth** annotated by doctors.

notes.definition: A mathematical function learned from data that turns inputs into predictions.
notes.example: The **model** predicts house prices from size and location.

notes.definition: A step-by-step procedure; in ML, the method used to learn a model from data.
notes.example: Random forest is a popular **algorithm** for tabular data.
notes.note: Ударение на первый слог: AL-go-ri-thm. Не путать с logarithm.

notes.definition: The output a model gives for a new input.
notes.example: The model's **predictions** were correct 92% of the time.

notes.definition: Learning from examples that come with correct answers (labels).
notes.example: Spam filtering is a classic **supervised learning** task.

notes.definition: Finding structure in data that has no labels.
notes.example: We used **unsupervised learning** to group customers by their behavior.

notes.definition: An agent learns by trial and error, receiving rewards or penalties for its actions.
notes.example: AlphaGo was trained with **reinforcement learning**.

notes.definition: Predicting which category an input belongs to.
notes.example: Deciding whether a tumor is benign or malignant is a **classification** problem.

notes.definition: Predicting a continuous number, such as a price or a temperature.
notes.example: We used **regression** to estimate the price of an apartment.

notes.definition: Grouping similar data points together without using labels.
notes.example: **Clustering** revealed three distinct types of users.

notes.definition: Compressing data into fewer features while keeping the important information.
notes.example: PCA is a common **dimensionality reduction** technique.

notes.definition: A data point that is very different from all the others.
notes.example: One **outlier** — an apartment priced at $10 million — distorted the average.

notes.definition: Random errors or irrelevant variation in data.
notes.example: Real-world data is full of **noise**.

notes.definition: The part of the data that the model learns from.
notes.example: We used 60% of the data as the **training set**.

notes.definition: Data held out to tune settings and choose the best model.
notes.example: Accuracy on the **validation set** stopped improving after ten epochs.

notes.definition: Data the model never sees during training, used only for the final evaluation.
notes.example: Never use the **test set** to tune your model.

notes.definition: When a model memorizes the training data, including its noise, and fails on new data.
notes.example: 99% on training data but 60% on new data — classic **overfitting**.

notes.definition: When a model is too simple to capture the real pattern in the data.
notes.example: A straight line can't follow this curve, so the model is **underfitting**.

notes.definition: To perform well on new data that the model has never seen.
notes.example: A good model **generalizes** to data it has never seen.

notes.definition: Too simple a model makes systematic errors (high bias); too complex a model is unstable (high variance). You balance the two.
notes.example: Choosing the depth of the tree is all about the **bias-variance trade-off**.

notes.definition: When information from the test data accidentally gets into training, making results look better than they really are.
notes.example: The suspiciously high score was caused by **data leakage**.

notes.definition: Creating useful input variables from raw data by hand.
notes.example: Good **feature engineering** often matters more than the choice of algorithm.

notes.definition: Cleaning and transforming raw data before training.
notes.example: **Preprocessing** took longer than training the model itself.

notes.definition: A simple model used as a reference point to compare other models against.
notes.example: Our neural network beat the **baseline** by 5%.

notes.definition: To let a model learn its parameters from data.
notes.example: It took two days to **train the model** on a single GPU.
notes.note: Модель именно train, а не teach.

notes.definition: A value the model learns during training, such as a weight.
notes.example: GPT-3 has 175 billion **parameters**.

notes.definition: A setting you choose before training, such as the learning rate or the number of layers.
notes.example: We spent a week tuning **hyperparameters**.

notes.definition: A formula that measures how wrong the model's predictions are.
notes.example: Training means minimizing the **loss function**.

notes.definition: An optimization method that repeatedly takes small steps downhill on the loss surface.
notes.example: **Gradient descent** slowly moves the weights toward the minimum.

notes.definition: How big each step of gradient descent is.
notes.example: If the **learning rate** is too high, training becomes unstable.

notes.definition: One full pass through the whole training dataset.
notes.example: We trained the network for 50 **epochs**.

notes.definition: A small group of examples processed together in one training step.
notes.example: With a **batch** size of 32, one epoch takes 300 steps.

notes.definition: (Of training) to settle at a stable, low value of the loss.
notes.example: After 20 epochs the loss finally **converged**.

notes.definition: The algorithm that updates the weights during training, for example Adam or SGD.
notes.example: Switching the **optimizer** to Adam sped up training.

notes.definition: Techniques that stop a model from becoming too complex, in order to fight overfitting.
notes.example: We added **regularization**, and the validation error dropped.

notes.definition: Stopping training as soon as performance on validation data stops improving.
notes.example: **Early stopping** saved us from overfitting.

notes.definition: Splitting the data into k parts and training k times, each time testing on a different part.
notes.example: We used five-fold **cross-validation** to get a reliable estimate.

notes.definition: The method that calculates how much each weight contributed to the error, going backward through the network.
notes.example: **Backpropagation** sends the error signal backward through the layers.

notes.definition: To train an already trained model a little more on your own, specific data.
notes.example: We **fine-tuned** a pre-trained model on medical texts.

notes.definition: The first, large-scale stage of training on huge amounts of general data.
notes.example: **Pre-training** on web text gives the model broad general knowledge.

notes.definition: Reusing knowledge learned on one task to solve another task.
notes.example: Thanks to **transfer learning**, we needed only 500 labeled images.

notes.definition: (ML slang) computing power: GPUs, time and money.
notes.example: Training frontier models requires an enormous amount of **compute**.
notes.note: Как существительное — жаргон; в эссе лучше computational resources. Часто произносят /ˈkɑːmpjuːt/.

notes.definition: To make something bigger: more data, more parameters, more compute.
notes.example: Performance kept improving as we **scaled up** the model.

notes.definition: Using a trained model to make predictions on new inputs.
notes.example: **Inference** is much cheaper than training.

notes.definition: The percentage of predictions that are correct.
notes.example: **Accuracy** can be misleading when one class is very rare.

notes.definition: Of all the items the model flagged as positive, the share that really are positive.
notes.example: High **precision** means few false alarms.

notes.definition: Of all the real positive cases, the share the model managed to find.
notes.example: For cancer screening, **recall** matters more than precision.

notes.definition: A single number that balances precision and recall (their harmonic mean).
notes.example: We report the **F1 score** because the classes are imbalanced.

notes.definition: A table showing correct and incorrect predictions for each class.
notes.example: The **confusion matrix** showed that the model often mixed up cats and foxes.

notes.definition: The model says “yes”, but the true answer is “no”.
notes.example: A **false positive** in spam filtering means a real email ends up in the spam folder.

notes.definition: The model says “no”, but the true answer is “yes”.
notes.example: In medicine, a **false negative** is dangerous: the disease is missed.

notes.definition: A plot of the true positive rate against the false positive rate at different thresholds.
notes.example: The area under the **ROC curve** (AUC) was 0.91.

notes.definition: The cut-off value above which a prediction counts as positive.
notes.example: Lowering the **threshold** increases recall but reduces precision.
notes.note: Пишется с одной h посередине: thres-hold.

notes.definition: A number used to measure how good a model is.
notes.example: Choose your **metric** before you start the experiment.

notes.definition: A standard test or dataset used to compare different models.
notes.example: The new model tops several reasoning **benchmarks**.

notes.definition: An experiment in which you remove parts of a system to see what each part contributes.
notes.example: An **ablation study** showed that most of the gain came from the attention layer.

notes.definition: A dataset in which one class is much rarer than the others.
notes.example: Fraud detection usually involves a highly **imbalanced dataset**.

notes.definition: Unlikely to be the result of pure chance.
notes.example: The improvement was small but **statistically significant**.

notes.definition: The best currently known results or methods.
notes.example: The model achieved **state-of-the-art** results on ImageNet.
notes.note: С дефисами — перед существительным: a state-of-the-art model.

notes.definition: A model made of layers of connected units, loosely inspired by the brain.
notes.example: **Neural networks** power modern speech recognition.

notes.definition: Machine learning with neural networks that have many layers.
notes.example: **Deep learning** made huge progress in computer vision after 2012.

notes.definition: A group of units in a neural network that process data at the same stage.
notes.example: The network has three hidden **layers**.

notes.definition: A number on a connection between neurons that the network learns during training.
notes.example: Training adjusts millions of **weights**.

notes.definition: A non-linear function applied to a neuron's output, such as ReLU or sigmoid.
notes.example: Without an **activation function**, the whole network would be just a linear model.

notes.definition: Randomly switching off some neurons during training to reduce overfitting.
notes.example: Adding **dropout** made the model more robust.

notes.definition: A problem where the learning signal becomes tiny in early layers, so they barely learn.
notes.example: Very deep networks used to suffer from the **vanishing gradient** problem.

notes.definition: A network that slides small filters over an image to detect patterns such as edges and shapes.
notes.example: **CNNs** are great at recognizing objects in photos.

notes.definition: A list of numbers representing a word or an item, so that similar things end up close together.
notes.example: In the **embedding** space, “king” and “queen” are close to each other.

notes.definition: A mechanism that lets a model focus on the most relevant parts of the input.
notes.example: **Attention** helps the model link “it” to the right noun.

notes.definition: A neural network architecture based on attention; the basis of modern language models.
notes.example: The **transformer** was introduced in the 2017 paper “Attention Is All You Need”.

notes.definition: The first part turns the input into an internal representation; the second turns that representation into the output.
notes.example: In translation, the **encoder** reads the Russian sentence and the **decoder** writes the English one.

notes.definition: The overall structure of a model: its layers and how they are connected.
notes.example: The team proposed a new **architecture** for video generation.

notes.definition: A processor that performs many calculations in parallel, ideal for training neural networks.
notes.example: We rented eight **GPUs** in the cloud.

notes.definition: A system whose inner workings are hard or impossible to understand.
notes.example: Deep neural networks are often criticized as **black boxes**.

notes.definition: In the internal workings of a machine or system.
notes.example: **Under the hood**, the chatbot is just predicting the next token.

notes.definition: AI that creates new content: text, images, audio or code.
notes.example: **Generative AI** can draft an essay in seconds.

notes.definition: A model that generates images by gradually removing noise from random pixels.
notes.example: Most modern image generators are **diffusion models**.

notes.definition: Able to work with several types of data, for example text, images and audio.
notes.example: A **multimodal** model can describe what's in a photo.

notes.definition: The field of teaching computers to understand images and video.
notes.example: Self-driving cars rely heavily on **computer vision**.

notes.definition: The field of making computers understand and produce human language.
notes.example: Chatbots and machine translation are **NLP** applications.

notes.definition: A huge neural network trained on text to predict what comes next.
notes.example: An **LLM** can summarize a long article in seconds.
notes.note: LLM читается по буквам: /ˌel el ˈem/.

notes.definition: A small piece of text — a word or part of a word — that a language model processes.
notes.example: The sentence was split into twelve **tokens**.

notes.definition: Splitting text into small pieces that a model can process.
notes.example: **Tokenization** works differently for English and Russian.

notes.definition: The maximum amount of text a model can take into account at once.
notes.example: The whole book didn't fit into the **context window**.

notes.definition: The instruction or text you give to a language model.
notes.example: A clear **prompt** gives much better answers.

notes.definition: Designing and refining instructions to get better results from a model.
notes.example: With careful **prompt engineering**, the answers became much more accurate.

notes.definition: Solving a task with no examples, or with just a few examples, given in the prompt.
notes.example: The model handled the task **zero-shot**, without a single example.

notes.definition: When a model confidently makes up false information.
notes.example: The citation looked real, but it was a **hallucination**.

notes.definition: Asking a model to reason step by step before giving the final answer.
notes.example: **Chain-of-thought** prompting improved accuracy on math problems.

notes.definition: A setting that controls how random or creative the model's output is.
notes.example: Use a low **temperature** for factual answers and a higher one for creative writing.

notes.ru: генерация с поиском по базе знаний
notes.definition: The model first searches a knowledge base, then writes an answer using what it found.
notes.example: We built a **RAG** system so the bot can answer questions about our documents.

notes.ru: согласование ИИ с целями и ценностями людей
notes.definition: Making AI systems behave according to human intentions and values.
notes.example: **Alignment** research tries to make AI systems safe and helpful.

notes.ru: обучение с подкреплением на отзывах людей
notes.definition: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: fine-tuning a model using people's ratings of its answers.
notes.example: **RLHF** made the chatbot more polite and helpful.

notes.definition: A system that plans and takes actions with tools to reach a goal on its own.
notes.example: The **AI agent** booked the meeting and sent the invitations by itself.

notes.definition: Rules and filters that keep an AI system's behavior safe.
notes.example: The company added **guardrails** to block harmful requests.

notes.definition: A model whose weights or code are publicly available.
notes.example: Many startups build their products on **open-source models**.

notes.definition: The time between sending a request and getting the response.
notes.example: Smaller models have lower **latency**.

notes.definition: A balance between two things, where getting more of one means getting less of the other.
notes.example: There's a **trade-off** between accuracy and speed.
colloc: a trade-off between X and Y

notes.definition: The training task of guessing which piece of text comes next.
notes.example: Surprisingly, **next-token prediction** leads to skills like translation and coding.

notes.definition: The observed rule that performance improves predictably with more data, parameters and compute.
notes.example: **Scaling laws** help labs plan the size of their next model.

notes.definition: Artificially generated data used for training or testing.
notes.example: We generated **synthetic data** to cover rare cases.

notes.definition: A trick prompt that makes a model ignore its safety rules.
notes.example: Researchers found a new **jailbreak** that bypassed the filters.

notes.term: fit a model to the data
notes.definition: To train a model so that it matches the data.
notes.example: We **fitted a linear model to the data**.

notes.definition: To adjust settings carefully to improve performance.
notes.example: We **tuned** the learning rate on the validation set.

notes.definition: To put a model or system into real use.
notes.example: The model was **deployed** to production last week.

notes.definition: To do better than someone or something else.
notes.example: Our approach **outperforms** previous methods by 3%.

notes.definition: To measure how good something is.
notes.example: We **evaluated** the model on three different datasets.

notes.definition: To carry out a test in order to find something out.
notes.example: We **ran an experiment** with different batch sizes.

notes.definition: To collect information for analysis.
notes.example: We **gathered data** from 500 volunteers.

notes.definition: To add labels or notes to data.
notes.example: Doctors **annotated** 2,000 X-ray images.

notes.definition: To use something to its maximum advantage.
notes.example: We **leverage** pre-trained models to save time.
notes.note: Бизнес-слово; в эссе часто лучше use / make use of. Британский вариант — /ˈliːvərɪdʒ/.

notes.definition: To make something bad less serious.
notes.example: Data augmentation helps **mitigate** overfitting.

notes.definition: To be likely to suffer from something.
notes.example: Large models **are prone to** overfitting on small datasets.

notes.definition: To depend a lot on something.
notes.example: The method **relies heavily on** high-quality labels.

notes.definition: To explain something, or to form a particular part of a total.
notes.example: The new feature **accounts for** most of the improvement.

notes.definition: To improve results noticeably.
notes.example: Combining several models **boosted performance** by 2%.

notes.definition: To be achieved only by losing something else.
notes.example: Higher accuracy **comes at the cost of** slower inference.

notes.definition: A setup in which people check or correct an AI system's decisions.
notes.example: Medical AI should keep a **human in the loop**.

notes.ru: мусор на входе — мусор на выходе
notes.definition: Bad input data inevitably leads to bad results.
notes.example: A model is only as good as its data: **garbage in, garbage out**.

notes.definition: To choose only the examples that support your point.
notes.example: The demo examples were clearly **cherry-picked**.

notes.definition: A quick test to make sure results are not obviously wrong.
notes.example: As a **sanity check**, we first trained on a tiny dataset.

notes.definition: A practical rule based on experience rather than exact theory.
notes.example: As a **rule of thumb**, start with a learning rate of 0.001.

notes.definition: Used before explaining something complicated in an easy way.
notes.example: **In simple terms**, a neural network is a very flexible function.

notes.term: The key idea behind X is …
notes.ru: ключевая идея X в том, что…
notes.definition: Introduces the main principle of a method or concept.
notes.example: **The key idea behind** gradient descent is to move downhill step by step.

notes.definition: The most important point is…
notes.example: In the end, **it all boils down to** the quality of the data.

notes.definition: Approximately, without going into details.
notes.example: **Roughly speaking**, the model guesses the most likely next word.

notes.definition: Introduces an important disadvantage.
notes.example: **One major drawback is** the huge energy consumption.

notes.definition: Introduces the opposite aspect of something (informal).
notes.example: AI saves time. **On the flip side**, it can make people less independent.
notes.note: Для эссе формальнее: On the other hand / However.

notes.definition: Draws attention to an important point.
notes.example: **It's worth noting that** the dataset was very small.

notes.definition: Introduces a possible problem or worry.
notes.example: Training on user chats **raises concerns about** privacy.

notes.definition: Something that has both advantages and disadvantages.
notes.example: Recommendation algorithms are **a double-edged sword**.
notes.note: В sword буква w не читается: /sɔːrd/.

notes.definition: To make a future development possible.
notes.example: Transformers **paved the way for** modern chatbots.

notes.definition: The most advanced at the moment.
notes.example: She works on **cutting-edge** research in robotics.

notes.definition: Something that completely changes a situation.
notes.example: Cheap GPUs were a **game-changer** for deep learning.

notes.definition: Over a long period of time in the future.
notes.example: **In the long run**, automation may create new types of jobs.

notes.definition: Partly; not completely.
notes.example: **To some extent**, AI already shapes the news we read.

notes.definition: More and more studies.
notes.example: **A growing body of research** suggests that AI tutors improve learning.

notes.term: It's only a matter of time before …
notes.definition: Something will definitely happen soon.
notes.example: **It's only a matter of time before** AI assistants become standard at work.

notes.definition: To stay at the same level or speed as something that changes fast.
notes.example: It's hard to **keep up with** how fast AI is developing.
colloc: keep up with the latest research

notes.definition: Exaggerated excitement about something.
notes.example: Not every AI startup lives up to the **hype**.

notes.definition: To be as good as people expected.
notes.example: The new model didn't **live up to expectations**.

notes.definition: Introduces your personal opinion.
notes.example: **From my perspective**, AI should support teachers, not replace them.

notes.definition: Using machines or software to do tasks instead of people.
notes.example: **Automation** has completely changed factory work.

notes.definition: The loss of jobs because machines or AI take over the work.
notes.example: Economists worry about **job displacement** in customer service.

notes.definition: To increase or improve something by adding to it.
notes.example: AI tools can **augment** doctors' abilities rather than replace them.

notes.definition: Unfair results caused by biased data or design.
notes.example: **Algorithmic bias** led the hiring tool to reject female candidates.

notes.definition: How well people can understand why a model made a particular decision.
notes.example: Banks need **explainability** to justify loan decisions.

notes.definition: Openness about how a system works and what data it uses.
notes.example: Users demand more **transparency** from AI companies.

notes.definition: Being responsible for decisions and their consequences.
notes.example: If a self-driving car crashes, who bears **accountability**?

notes.definition: The right to keep personal information protected.
notes.example: Training on user chats raises **privacy** issues.

notes.definition: Close monitoring of people, often by governments or companies.
notes.example: Facial recognition makes mass **surveillance** much easier.

notes.definition: False information that spreads, often without the intention to deceive.
notes.example: AI can generate **misinformation** at scale.

notes.definition: A realistic fake video or audio recording created with AI.
notes.example: A **deepfake** of the politician went viral.

notes.definition: Official rules that control an activity.
notes.example: The EU AI Act is the first major **regulation** of AI.

notes.definition: Worries about whether something is morally right.
notes.example: **Ethical concerns** around AI include bias, privacy and safety.

notes.definition: The gap between people who have access to technology and those who don't.
notes.example: AI could widen the **digital divide**.

notes.definition: To learn new skills for a different job / to improve skills for your current one.
notes.example: Workers will need to **reskill** as AI changes their jobs.

notes.definition: Understanding what AI can and can't do, and how to use it responsibly.
notes.example: Schools should start teaching **AI literacy**.
